description:
A major incident has been declared in the UK near RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the US military. Police have arrested several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. Homes near the base in Gloucestershire were evacuated, and residents were taken to a nearby leisure centre. Army bomb disposal experts are examining a number of vehicles in the area. Armed police have cordoned off the area around RAF Fairford, about 100 kilometres west of London. About 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were deployed. Police say they believe the incident is contained, with counter-terrorism police leading the investigation. RAF Fairford has strategic importance for US and NATO operations and was used by US forces to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites. Security has also been tightened at other RAF bases across the UK as a precaution. 

Al Jazeera’s Frances Read reports from London.

Two separate mass shootings in South Africa have killed at least 27 people, with 17 killed at a tavern southwest of Johannesburg and 10 killed at an entertainment venue near Cape Town. Police are searching for the gunmen, and no arrests have been reported and the motives remain unclear. 
In an interview with Al Jazeera, journalist Velani Ludidi says, the two attacks are not believed to be linked. He attributed the wider rise in mass shootings to the proliferation of illegal firearms and entrenched organised crime, while warning that corruption and weak crime intelligence are hampering efforts to tackle the problem. Ludidi said gangs are also exploiting poverty and inequality to recruit young people, including children, into criminal networks. He argued that South Africa needs stronger investigations, better cooperation between police and communities, and improved crime intelligence to prevent further attacks. title: South Africa mass shootings kill at least 27 as illegal guns fuel mass violence, journalist says

description:
A suicide bomber targeted a police and customs checkpoint in Dera Ismail Khan in northwestern Pakistan on Saturday, killing at least 12 people and injuring 35 others. The attack involved a vehicle-borne explosive device that was rammed into the checkpoint, which is in a strategically important area linking Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan and Punjab. Gunmen later targeted an ambulance responding to the blast, according to the report. The victims included security personnel and passersby, with women and children among those killed and wounded. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, although Pakistani security sources have pointed to the Pakistani Taliban, or TTP, as a possible perpetrator. Pakistan has accused the Afghan Taliban government of providing safe haven to armed groups and has carried out cross-border strikes into Afghanistan in response to attacks it says originate there. 

Al Jazeera’s Osama Bin Javaid reports from Islamabad.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Iran is increasingly shifting trade from maritime routes to land borders as restrictions on access to its southern ports disrupt imports. The change is putting growing pressure on border crossings with neighbouring countries, particularly the main crossing with Turkiye, where truck queues now stretch for kilometres and delays can last days or even weeks. Truck drivers say journeys that once took a day can now take a week, while some report making only one or two trips every several weeks. Iran's customs authority says imports through the Gurbulak crossing rose 250 percent in the five months to August. Before the war, more than 80 percent of Iran's trade moved through its southern ports, but maritime restrictions are forcing Tehran to rely more heavily on road and rail links. Iran and Turkiye are working to ease congestion, but limited land capacity and higher transport costs are adding pressure on businesses and consumers. 

Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu reports from Tehran.

title: Iran turns to land trade as US naval blockade leaves trucks stuck for weeks at Turkiye border

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
More than 10,000 troops have been deployed in Bangkok to help evacuate residents caught up in major flooding, after all 50 of the Thai capital's districts were declared disaster zones. Heavy rain has overwhelmed the city's drainage systems, and temporary shelters have been set up for more than 4,000 people forced from their homes.

Residents are frustrated that lessons from Bangkok's 2011 floods, including calls to clean out canals and improve irrigation, were never fully acted on, leaving the same infrastructure under strain again. A similar crisis hit the southern city of Hat Yai last year. Residents say they don't expect the government to control the rain, but want more effective, better-prepared administrations, as more heavy rain is forecast.

Al Jazeera's Tony Cheng reports from Bangkok.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Ross Harrison, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute and author of Decoding Iran's Foreign Policy, says Iran likely expected President Donald Trump to reject its seven-day proposal, since it largely repackages the framework agreed by Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron in a June memorandum of understanding that Washington later tried to undermine.

Harrison says Iran's goal was less about winning US approval than showing its own public, and the American public, a willingness to negotiate. He sees a possible concession in language suggesting the Strait of Hormuz could reopen without ships needing to coordinate with Tehran, a key sticking point that helped collapse the original deal, but says Iran is also working to secure a post-war toll structure with Gulf Arab states.

The US, Harrison says, believes it got a bad deal in June and is betting economic pressure will pay off given time, with Trump's aides reportedly signalling a status quo until after the US midterm elections
title: Why Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz proposal: Analysis
